venues.a: Staré Město (Old Town), on the Vltava riverbank
venues.d: Three linked historic houses — Baroque, Renaissance and neo-Classical — on the river, with the finest Castle-and-bridge view in the city.

venues.a: Staré Město (Old Town), by the river near the Jewish Quarter
venues.d: A landmark riverfront grande dame reborn under Fairmont — the only hotel in Prague to earn two MICHELIN Keys.

venues.a: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
venues.d: A former 14th-century monastery turned serene Mandarin Oriental house, quietly hidden in the cobbled lanes beneath the Castle.

venues.a: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), by the Augustinian monastery
venues.d: Woven around a still-working 13th-century Augustinian monastery — cloisters, a monk's brewery, and Cubist-inspired design.
Set in the restored 1916 Sugar Palace — a design-led Hyatt house threading 1920s retro-futurist Czech art through the historic centre.

venues.a: Nové Město (New Town), near Wenceslas Square
venues.d: A restored 1932 Art Deco landmark — the storied Alcron reborn, with its glamorous heritage dining room, Brasserie 1932.
A former Baroque palace with one of the largest private hotel gardens in the Old Town — classical grandeur, quietly kept.

venues.a: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), by St Nicholas Church
venues.d: A music-themed boutique below the Castle, each floor devoted to a genre — with a rooftop terrace over the red rooftops of the Lesser Town.
A cluster of Renaissance and Baroque townhouses restored with gilded, theatrical opulence — an ornate, old-world hideaway.
A discreet contemporary design hotel a few steps from the Old Town Square — a rooftop lounge, a library, and a quietly modern hand.
The first restaurant devoted to Czech cuisine to win a MICHELIN star — a long tasting menu reviving 19th-century Bohemian cookbooks.
Radek Kašpárek's playful, farm-driven modern cooking — Prague's most consistently celebrated star, and a MICHELIN Service Award winner.
Chef Matteo de Carli cooking the food of his Italian homeland — handmade pasta at the counter, and Prague's newest MICHELIN star.
Christian Chu's Nordic technique laced with Asian spice — an inventive, individual tasting menu that won a star in 2025.
Martin Štangl's manifesto for modern Czech cooking — foraged herbs and forgotten ingredients, and both a MICHELIN Star and Green Star.
Barbora Šimůnková's sustainability-led kitchen — a MICHELIN Green Star for produce-forward, low-waste cooking.

venues.a: Nové Město (New Town), V Jirchářích, near the National Theatre
venues.d: A day-to-night gastronomic complex — café, restaurant and one of Europe's most acclaimed bars — with a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand kitchen.
Confident, generous modern Czech cooking that has held its Bib Gourmand — a favourite of the local dining crowd.
A polished neighbourhood restaurant with Italian leanings — reliably good, and a long-standing Bib Gourmand.
Czech and French cooking on a quiet hill in Smíchov — a warm, well-priced Bib Gourmand off the tourist map.
Modern Czech cooking with a serious approach to Czech beer — a fresh Bib Gourmand doing the classics properly.
An assured, ingredient-led kitchen that earned a Bib Gourmand in the guide's first Czechia edition.
A refined take on Czech classics in a smart neighbourhood room — a new Bib Gourmand for 2025.
A bakery-and-restaurant landmark of the Karlín revival — modern Czech cooking, wood-fired bread, and a MICHELIN listing.

venues.a: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
venues.d: A rooftop dining terrace with one of the great Prague views — the Castle and the red rooftops laid out below.

The largest coherent castle complex in the world by Guinness reckoning, a thousand years of palaces, courtyards and cathedral spires crowning the skyline above the river. A private early-access tour before the gates open lets a multi-generational family have the courtyards almost to themselves.

Nearly six centuries in the building, this soaring Gothic cathedral inside the castle walls holds the Bohemian crown jewels, royal tombs and the shimmering Art Nouveau windows Alfons Mucha designed. The 287-step climb of the Great South Tower rewards with the finest close view over the whole city.

The 14th-century stone bridge lined with thirty Baroque saints, linking the Old Town to the castle side across the Vltava. Cross at dawn — before the crowds and buskers arrive — for the postcard light on the water and the towers, an unhurried moment that suits early-rising elders and children alike.

The medieval heart of Prague, ringed by pastel Gothic and Baroque facades, the twin spires of Týn Church and pavement cafes. A grand, walkable stage for the whole family, with the Astronomical Clock chiming on the hour.

venues.n: Prague Astronomical Clock & Old Town Hall (Orloj)
venues.d: One of the oldest working astronomical clocks in the world, dating to 1410, with a procession of the Twelve Apostles that draws a crowd every hour. Climb the Old Town Hall tower for a bird's-eye sweep of the square and its rooftops — a lift makes it easy for less mobile travellers.

The most complete surviving complex of Jewish monuments in Europe, its historic synagogues and cemetery woven into the Old Town. A guided walk through seven centuries of Prague's Jewish story is one of the city's most moving and reflective experiences for a family.

The oldest active synagogue in Europe, in continuous use since around 1270, and the legendary home of the Golem myth. Its austere early-Gothic hall is unlike anything else in the city — small, atmospheric and still a living house of prayer.

A dazzling Moorish-Revival interior of gilded arabesques, stained glass and a starry domed ceiling — the most sumptuous of all Prague's synagogues, part of the Jewish Museum. Intimate evening chamber concerts here are a discreet, refined way to spend an hour.

Twelve thousand weathered headstones tilting against each other in layered rows, one of the most evocative burial grounds in the world, used from the 15th to the 18th century. A quiet, thought-provoking stop within the Jewish Museum circuit.

Prague's Baroque quarter beneath the castle, its noble palaces, hidden courtyards and cobbled lanes barely changed since the 18th century. The perfect district for an unhurried private walk, with quiet corner cafes and garden restaurants for a mid-stroll pause.

venues.n: St Nicholas Church, Malá Strana (Kostel sv. Mikuláše)
venues.d: The supreme masterpiece of Prague Baroque, a vast green dome and a ceiling fresco so grand it seems to open the roof to heaven. Time a visit to one of the frequent organ or chamber concerts held beneath the dome.

venues.n: Church of Our Lady before Týn (Chrám Matky Boží před Týnem)
venues.d: The twin black Gothic spires rising over Old Town Square are the defining silhouette of medieval Prague, each crowned with a crown of mini-spires. The astronomer Tycho Brahe lies buried inside this soaring, dimly lit interior.

A jewel-box Baroque pilgrimage shrine near the castle, built around a replica of the Holy House, with a famous treasury of monstrances glittering with thousands of diamonds. Its cloister and carillon of bells make it a peaceful counterpoint to the busier castle.

Two of the most beautiful Baroque library halls on earth — the Theological and Philosophical Halls — with painted ceilings, antique globes and a cabinet of curiosities. The hilltop terrace outside offers one of the best panoramas of the spired city below.

A jaw-dropping 1727 Jesuit library hall of frescoed ceilings and historic globes, reached only by guided tour, plus a climb up the Astronomical Tower for a wraparound view over the Old Town rooftops. The small-group entry keeps it calm and civilised.

A row of tiny brightly-painted 16th-century cottages tucked inside the castle walls, once home to castle marksmen and later, briefly, to Franz Kafka at No. 22. A charming, storybook lane that delights children and grandparents alike.

The finest Art Nouveau building in Prague, a 1912 confection of mosaics, stained glass and interiors decorated by Mucha and his peers, wrapped around the grand Smetana concert hall. A guided tour of the salons, then dinner in the opulent French restaurant, makes an elegant evening.

The world's first museum devoted to Alfons Mucha, the Czech master whose sinuous posters of flowing-haired Slavic women defined Art Nouveau. A compact, intimate collection a short walk from Wenceslas Square — an easy, rewarding hour for art lovers of any age.

venues.n: The Slav Epic by Alfons Mucha (at the Municipal House)
venues.d: Mucha's monumental twenty-canvas cycle telling the saga of the Slavic peoples, some panels the size of a cinema screen, now on show inside the Municipal House. A single, awe-inspiring encounter with a national masterpiece.

A wooded 327-metre hill of orchards and rose gardens crowned by a miniature Eiffel-style tower with a 360-degree view of Prague. A gentle, green escape from the streets below, with a mirror maze and observatory that keep younger travellers happy.

A wooded plateau above the river where a giant metronome now stands on the old plinth that once held a Stalin statue, and where you can count seven of Prague's bridges in one sweep. The seasonal beer garden with its Old Town view is a beloved local sunset spot.

The classic way to see the castle, Charles Bridge and the National Theatre reflected in the water, from a leisurely daytime glide to a candlelit dinner cruise at night. A private charter with a chef briefed on vegetarian and Jain preferences is easily arranged.

Nicknamed 'Prague's Venice' for its little canal and waterwheel, this leafy island beneath Charles Bridge holds a riverside park and the ever-changing John Lennon Wall of painted messages. A relaxed, romantic wander with the Kampa modern-art museum alongside.

A converted riverside mill housing a fine collection of Central European modern art, strong on František Kupka and the Cubist sculptor Otto Gutfreund. A calm, well-curated space with a terrace café looking straight across the Vltava.

A grand early-Baroque garden of clipped hedges, a dramatic frescoed grotto and bronze statues, hidden behind the walls of a palace that is now the Czech Senate — and free to enter. Peacocks roam the lawns, delighting children, and it is blissfully quiet.

One of the most beautiful terraced Baroque gardens in Central Europe, climbing in ornamental tiers up the hillside with statues and a view over the red roofs of the Lesser Town. A serene, little-known hideaway ideal for a private moment.

The exquisite 1783 Classical theatre where Mozart himself conducted the world premiere of Don Giovanni in 1787, still staging the opera today in near-original surroundings. To hear Mozart in the very room he wrote it for is one of Europe's great cultural experiences.

The gilded neo-Renaissance temple of Czech culture on the riverbank, its golden roof a landmark, staging opera, ballet and drama beneath a ceiling of allegorical paintings. A box for an evening performance is a grand, memorable night out.

One of the finest 19th-century concert halls on the continent, whose Dvořák Hall is home to the world-class Czech Philharmonic. A ticket here is the connoisseur's choice for classical music in Prague, in a riverside setting of real grandeur.

A sumptuously restored neo-Rococo opera house near the top of Wenceslas Square, staging grand opera and ballet under a lavishly painted auditorium. The recent renovation returned it to full jewel-box splendour.

Prague's distinctive black-light theatre, where UV-lit figures float and transform against a black stage in wordless, dreamlike shows. Because it needs no language, it is a genuinely fun, all-ages evening for multi-generational groups.

A cliff-top fortress above the Vltava, wrapped around the neo-Gothic Church of Sts Peter and Paul, ancient ramparts and the Slavín cemetery where Dvořák, Smetana and Mucha lie. Far quieter than the castle, with sweeping river views and space for children to run.

venues.n: National Gallery — Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác)
venues.d: Prague's great museum of modern and contemporary art, in a landmark 1928 Functionalist building, with works by Picasso, Klimt, Van Gogh and Mucha's Slav Epic hall. The single most important art collection in the country, and rarely crowded.

A sharp, converted-factory space for cutting-edge contemporary art, architecture and design, crowned by the Gulliver airship — a huge wooden zeppelin on the roof. The most forward-looking cultural stop in the city, with a good design shop and café.

venues.n: Wenceslas Square & the National Museum (Václavské náměstí)
venues.d: The grand boulevard-square at the heart of modern Prague, scene of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, closed at its top by the newly restored, palatial National Museum. History, shopping and grand architecture in one broad sweep.

A stately residential quarter of Art Nouveau apartment blocks, leafy squares and the city's best independent restaurants and wine bars — regularly named among the world's coolest neighbourhoods. The relaxed, refined district in which discerning travellers actually want to spend an evening.

A rolling park in Vinohrady whose grassy slope offers a classic view of the castle and spires at sunset, home to one of Prague's largest and most beloved beer gardens. A local, easygoing way to end a warm day.

Prague's tallest structure and its most divisive landmark, a 216-metre space-age tower with crawling giant baby sculptures by David Černý and a 360-degree observation deck. There's a one-room luxury suite and a restaurant near the top for a memorable, offbeat treat.

A once-industrial district reborn after the 2002 floods into one of Prague's leading quarters for design, cuisine and cafés, anchored by the grand neo-Romanesque Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius. The place to see contemporary, creative Prague away from the tourist core.

The revived Vltava embankment of vaulted cellar bars and moored boats, with a lively Saturday farmers' market of Czech produce, cheeses and street food. A genuinely local scene with castle-and-bridge views, and plenty of vegetarian-friendly stalls.

The last surviving open-air market in the historic core, trading since 1232, with stalls of fruit, flowers, wooden toys and Czech crafts. A quick, atmospheric stop between the Old Town Square and the river.

A soaring blackened-Gothic gate tower marking the start of the medieval coronation route to the castle, standing beside the Art Nouveau Municipal House in a striking clash of eras. A short climb gives a fine view down the Royal Way.

A former silver-mining boomtown an hour east, home to the soaring Gothic St Barbara's Cathedral and the extraordinary Sedlec Ossuary, a chapel decorated with the bones of tens of thousands. An unforgettable, easily private half- or full-day excursion.

A storybook medieval town cradled in a bend of the Vltava, all pastel houses, cobbled lanes and a vast hilltop castle with its own Baroque theatre. Worth an overnight rather than a rush; a private car and guide turn the long drive into an unhurried pleasure.

The grand 19th-century spa town of colonnades, thermal springs and pastel promenades where emperors and composers once took the cure, and the home of Becherovka liqueur and Moser crystal. A refined day of mineral springs, café society and a spa treatment for the whole party.
A dark, intimate cocktail den devoted to Hemingway — rare rums, an absinthe fountain, and some of the most inventive drinks in the city.
Cocktails and Champagne given equal billing — exposed brick, chandeliers, candlelight, and one of the largest Champagne lists in the world.
Prague's most decorated bar — wild herbs, foraged ingredients and pickled pine cones in the glass, in a converted former cinema.

venues.a: Staré Město (Old Town), beneath the U Prince Hotel on Old Town Square
venues.d: A Prohibition-era cocktail cellar in a Gothic vault right on the Old Town Square — barrel-aged classics served on hand-made Moser glass.

venues.a: Nové Město (New Town), atop the Hilton Prague
venues.d: A glass-walled sky bar and terrace over the Vltava — one of the few genuine high-level views in a city of low rooftops.

venues.a: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
venues.d: A rooftop terrace tucked beneath Prague Castle — the Baroque rooftops and spires of the Lesser Town laid out at your feet.
